subject: hedgehog
pitch: A plump hedgehog out on an autumn evening walk. A dome of spines in chestnut brown with cream tips, a soft fawn face with a pointed, twitchy snout, a shiny black button nose, tiny round ears and bright beady eyes. Little pink paws, and a single red maple leaf stuck on its spines like a trophy.
reasoning:
I need to produce a single TypeScript module using the agentic-3js-builder SDK, but I only have partial documentation for its API. I should be careful to stick strictly to the documented helpers I know, like createBuilder, joint, chain, and sweep, rather than inventing functions that may not exist.

I'm cataloguing the rest of the builder's surface area: membrane, along, rod/capsule/frustumBox, slab, loft, limb, spike, part, extrude, lathe, stick, sprout, cards, ring, pose, and surface with its nearest/around/ray/scatter/loop/drape methods, plus decal and region. I'm also noting the geometry helpers like frame, line, aim, lerp, and paint utilities like countershade, spots, and stripes.

I'm unsure about the exact signature for b.part's geometry argument -- likely it takes a raw THREE.Geometry instance like a SphereGeometry alongside a color and placement options.

I'm reasoning through how aim and dir might orient a part's axis for cylinders or cones, and what object type b.surface expects as input -- possibly a Part or Sweep. I'm also uncertain whether scatter takes a rng argument for determinism, and since I can't pin down scatter's exact signature, I'm leaning toward avoiding it and instead placing things explicitly using surface.around(center).at(azimuth, elevation), though I'm still unsure whether azimuth and elevation are in radians or degrees.

Instead I'm considering surface.ray(origin, dir) or surface.nearest(point), both of which take clearly documented Point inputs and return a Hit, which seems like a safer bet. For spikes, I'm working through b.spike(base, dirOrTip, len, r), where base can be a Hit since Hits convert to Points via their Frame position, and I'm thinking about whether b.stick() could seat a cone geometry along a hit's normal direction for building spine-like protrusions on the surface.

For the cream-tipped spines, I'm leaning toward using spike for the main brown spine, then stacking a shorter cream spike near the tip—offsetting its base further along the direction vector with a reduced length and radius so it reads as a tip cap rather than a separate shape.

But doubling parts per spine worries me given the roughly 1000-part budget, so I need to limit spine counts carefully, maybe around 120 brown plus matching cream caps, rather than going for hundreds of spines that would blow the budget. I'm also wondering whether merging geometries manually via a Three.js utility is viable, but that import path seems risky, so I'll plan to just keep total spine counts modest instead.

I'm also second-guessing whether to build the dome surface procedurally with `b.surface(body)` and its nearest-point lookup, versus computing spine base points myself analytically on an ellipsoid using normals, since the latter avoids relying on uncertain API behavior for surface sampling on a built body.

Spine rigidity should follow the body's bone automatically since nothing-tuples attach to the closest bone, so I don't need to specify a bone explicitly for `b.spike`.

Now I'm shifting toward the overall model design: sizing the hedgehog stylized but proportionate (body ~0.3m long, ~0.2m tall), facing +Z, standing at y=0, and sketching out the joint hierarchy starting from a root.

Working through the skeleton naming: root joint ("body" or "hips") positioned near y=0.1-0.11, with parent-child relationships for subsequent joints like the head, though I'm still uncertain about the exact syntax for specifying parent in the joint API.

For the head and face, I'm leaning toward a sphere combined with a forward-pointing cone to form the pointed snout, rather than a more complex sweep or loft, keeping things simple with primitive shapes and scaling.

Rather than rely on an uncertain `scale` option in the `b.part` API, I'll scale the three.js geometries directly before passing them in—this avoids guessing the exact parameter format and is guaranteed to work with standard three.js methods. For the snout cone, I'm figuring out how to orient it so its tip points forward, likely using the `dir` option to aim the geometry's axis correctly.

Confirming bone takes the joint object directly, with no dir defaulting to identity orientation. Now I'm working out the body geometry as a plump ellipsoid centered around (0, 0.15, -0.02) with radii roughly 0.13 x, 0.12 y, 0.17 z, positioning it so the belly sits just above the ground since short legs will bridge the gap to the paws on the floor.

Adjusting so the body center sits at y=0.13 with ry=0.11, leaving the bottom slightly above ground, with pink paw capsules extending from the floor up to meet the belly. Spines will cover the dome's upper hemisphere and sides but avoid the belly and the fawn-colored face region at the front (+Z), using normal-vector thresholds to carve out the face zone. I'm planning roughly 110 spine positions distributed via a Fibonacci sphere pattern, each with a cream tip (so ~220 parts total), plus separate parts for the face, ears, eyes, nose, paws, and a small red maple leaf accessory stuck on the back.

For the leaf, I'll avoid relying on an uncertain custom extrude helper and instead build it with plain three.js: define a 2D leaf-lobed shape and run it through ExtrudeGeometry for a flat shape with slight depth, which I can then place and orient myself. I'll impale the leaf onto the spines at the top of the back, tilted like a trophy, possibly adding a thin dark stem spike piece that visually pierces into the leaf and spines for a stuck-on look.

Now I'm working out the maple leaf outline itself, sketching lobe tip angles and radii around a polar coordinate approximation to get a recognizable five-lobed silhouette for the shape points.

Working out the leaf's tip and notch angles going counterclockwise...

I'm settling on 10 points total, alternating tips (radius ~1.0) and notches (radius 0.3-0.5) around the shape. For paws, I'm placing small pink ellipsoid feet at the front and back corners of the body, connected by short stubby fawn-colored legs. I'm leaning toward a joint-based limb structure so each paw lands precisely at its target position under the body.

To avoid uncertainty around cylinder orientation and the `dir`/`aim` parameters, I'll stick to spheres for the legs rather than risk misaligned rod shapes.

Thinking about bone ownership: since bones belong to the parent joint, geometry near the body-to-head bone attributes to body, and similarly limb bones nearest their attachment point default to the parent joint — so spines on top of the body should resolve to the body bone correctly without needing explicit assignment.

For the spines themselves, I'm sketching them as slender tapered cones with a brown base and a cream tip cap offset slightly inward for a visible color step, keeping them thin and pointed to read as stylized spikes.

Distributing roughly 120 spines using a Fibonacci spiral over the sphere surface, then filtering by normal direction to keep them on the back and sides while excluding the fawn-colored front face and head region near the forehead.

I'm reconsidering the spine spacing and count—bumping to around 260 Fibonacci points before filtering to get roughly 150+ spines with ~0.037m spacing, which feels readable but still sparse enough to look natural. I'm now weighing whether to actually use the rng utility or switch to a deterministic index-based formula instead—since I'm unsure of the exact rng API, a hash-like deterministic approach avoids guessing wrong while still giving varied, natural-looking lengths without technically violating the randomness requirement if I just skip using randomness altogether.

For colors, I'm settling on a flat, warm autumn palette for the hedgehog: chestnut brown body and spine base, cream spine tips, fawn face, dark nose and eyes with white highlights, darker fawn ears with pink inner ears, pink paws, and a red maple leaf with a brown stem caught in its spines, keeping everything as simple flat colors without relying on uncertain texture/paint APIs.

I'm skipping any extra ground patch or props to keep focus on the hedgehog itself, then working out precise placement math for the eyes on the curved head surface—calculating offset vectors so they sit just embedded in the skull at the right radius—and now I'm figuring out how the pointed snout cone should angle forward from the head.

Working out the nose sphere's position at the snout tip, then figuring out ear placement as thin flattened spheres oriented outward from the sides of the head, with small pink inner-ear shapes layered on top.

Trying to position that belly sphere so it only peeks out below the spine dome without clipping into the chestnut body is getting messy -- the two shapes keep overlapping and causing z-fighting, so I'm leaning toward dropping the separate belly piece entirely and just letting the fawn coloring live on the face instead.
